'''Nergis Mavalvala''' (born 1968) is a Pakistani-American [[astrophysicist]]. She is the Curtis and Kathleen Marble Professor of [[Astrophysics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where she is also the dean of the university's [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology School of Science|school of science]]. She was previously the Associate Head of the university's [[MIT Department of Physics|Department of Physics]].<ref name="MIT">{{cite web|title=Nergis Mavalvala - MIT Department of Physics|url=http://web.mit.edu/physics/people/faculty/mavalvala_nergis.html|website=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|access-date=18 February 2016}}</ref> Mavalvala is best known for her work on the detection of gravitational waves in the [[LIGO|Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory]] (LIGO) project,<ref name="MIT" /><ref name="TheHindu">{{cite news |last1=Krishnan |first1=Madhuvanti S. |date=25 February 2016 |title=Making waves |website=The Hindu |url=https://www.thehindu.com/features/kids/read-about-nergis-mavalvala-who-made-the-news-last-week/article8280169.ece |access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref> and for the exploration and experimental demonstration of [[Macroscopic quantum phenomena|macroscopic]] [[Quantum mechanics|quantum]] effects such as [[Squeezed coherent state|squeezing]] in [[Cavity optomechanics|optomechanics]]. She was awarded a [[MacArthur Fellow]]ship in 2010.<ref name="MacArthur Foundation">{{cite web|title=Nergis Mavalvala - MacArthur Foundation|url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/35/|website=MacArthur Foundation|access-date=18 February 2016}}</ref><ref name="AutoStraddle">{{cite web|title=Nergis Mavalvala and Five Exceptional Stories Of Women In STEM|url=https://www.autostraddle.com/nergis-mavalvala-and-five-exceptional-stories-of-women-in-stem-329015/|website=AutoStraddle|date=24 February 2016|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Chu |first1=Jennifer |title=Nergis Mavalvala named School of Science dean |url=http://news.mit.edu/2020/nergis-mavalvala-science-dean-0817 |website=MIT |date=17 August 2020 |access-date=18 August 2020}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Mavalvala was born in [[Lahore]], but primarily raised in [[Karachi]], Pakistan.<ref name="Nergis Mavalvala named School of Science dean">{{cite web|title=Nergis Mavalvala named School of Science dean|url=http://news.mit.edu/2020/nergis-mavalvala-science-dean-0817|access-date=18 August 2020|website=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=17 August 2020 }}</ref> Born to a [[Parsi]] family that practiced [[Zoroastrianism]], Mavalvala was the younger of the two children.<ref name="TheHindu" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Rehman |first=Atika |date=2016-02-15 |title=Nergis Mavalvala, Pakistan's unexpected celebrity scientist |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1239667 |access-date=2021-12-03 |website=DAWN.COM |language=en}}</ref> She attended the [[Convent of Jesus and Mary, Karachi|Convent of Jesus and Mary]], [[Karachi]], where she received her [[GCE Ordinary Level|O-Level]] and later, moved to the United States in 1986 and enrolled at [[Wellesley College]], where she received a [[bachelor's degree]] in physics and [[astronomy]] in 1990. She then joined [[Rainer Weiss]]'s group in the MIT physics department and received her [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] in 1997.

== Career ==
As a graduate student at MIT, she conducted her doctoral work under [[Rainer Weiss]], developing a prototype laser interferometer for detecting gravitational waves.<ref name="TEDxCLE">{{cite web|title=Nergis Mavalvala|url=http://www.tedxcle.com/nergis-mavalvala/|website=TEDxCLE|access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>  After graduate school, she worked as a [[postdoctoral researcher]] and then as a research scientist at the [[California Institute of Technology]], starting her work with [[cosmic microwave background]],<ref>{{cite news |title=Pakistan-born scientist played part in discovery of gravitational waves |url=https://tribune.com.pk/story/1046004/scientific-breakthrough-pakistan-born-scientist-played-part-in-discovery/ |work=The Express Tribune |date=12 February 2016 |language=en}}</ref> and eventually working on the LIGO.<ref name="ScienceMag">{{cite web |date=June 2012 |title=Gravitational wave researcher succeeds by being herself |url=http://www.sciencemag.org/careers/2012/06/just-herself |access-date=18 February 2016 |website=ScienceMag - AAAS}}</ref> Mavalvala focuses primarily on two fields of physics: [[Gravitational-wave astronomy|Gravitational-wave astrophysics]] and quantum measurement science.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://emvogil-3.mit.edu/~nergis/|title=Welcome to the Page of Nergis Mavalvala|access-date=8 April 2018|archive-date=3 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200703201055/https://emvogil-3.mit.edu/~nergis/|url-status=dead}}</ref> Mavalvala joined the MIT physics faculty in 2002.<ref name="ScienceMag" /> In 2017 she was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Press release: National Academy of Sciences elects six MIT professors for 2017|url=https://news.mit.edu/2017/nas-elects-six-mit-professors-0503|work=MIT News|date=3 May 2017}}</ref>

=== Detection of gravitational waves ===

Mavalvala was part of the team of scientists who, for the first time, detected ripples in the fabric of [[spacetime]] known as [[gravitational wave]]s. Mavalvala has been working on gravitational waves since 1991.<ref name=":1" /> After the announcement of the observation, she became an instant celebrity scientist in her birthplace of Pakistan. A statement by the [[Prime Minister of Pakistan]] [[Nawaz Sharif]] praised Mavalvala, calling her a source of inspiration for Pakistani scientists and students aspiring to become future scientists. He also stated that ''"the entire nation is proud of her valuable contribution."''<ref>{{cite web|title=PM praises Pakistani scientist who played key role in discovery of gravitational waves|url=http://tribune.com.pk/story/1047451/pm-congratulates-pakistani-who-played-part-in-discovery-of-gravitational-waves/|website=Express Tribune|date=15 February 2016 |access-date=18 February 2016}}</ref>

On 20 February 2016, [[Pakistan Ambassador to the United States|Ambassador of Pakistan to the United States]], [[Jalil Abbas Jilani]], conveyed the [[Government of Pakistan]]'s message of felicitation to Mavalvala for her outstanding achievement in the field of astrophysics. He also invited her to re-visit Pakistan, which she accepted.<ref name="DAWN">{{cite web |date=15 February 2016 |title=Nergis Mavalvala, Pakistan's unexpected celebrity scientist |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/1239667/ |access-date=18 February 2016 |website=DAWN}}</ref><ref name="PakistanObserver">{{cite web|title=Prof Dr Nergis Mavalvala to Visit Pakistan|url=http://pakobserver.net/2016/02/20/prof-dr-nergis-mavalvala-to-visit-pakistan/|website=Pakistan Observer|access-date=25 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303121431/http://pakobserver.net/2016/02/20/prof-dr-nergis-mavalvala-to-visit-pakistan/|archive-date=3 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="RadioPakistan">{{cite web|title=Jilani conveys PM's greetings to Pakistani-US scientist|url=http://www.radio.gov.pk/newsdetail/82836/1|website=Radio Pakistan|access-date=25 February 2016|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160301052708/http://www.radio.gov.pk/newsdetail/82836/1|archive-date=1 March 2016|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref name="ET3">{{cite web|title=Would Nergis Mavalvala have made it had she stayed in Pakistan?|url=http://blogs.tribune.com.pk/story/32394/would-nergis-mavalvala-have-made-it-had-she-stayed-in-pakistan/|website=The Express Tribune|date=16 February 2016 |access-date=25 February 2016}}</ref>

=== Laser cooling ===

Optical cooling of mirrors to nearly [[absolute zero]] can help eliminate [[Noise (signal processing)|measurement noise]] arising from thermal vibrations.  A portion of Mavalvala's work focused on the extension of laser-cooling techniques to optically cool and trap more and more [[mass]]ive objects, both for the LIGO project and for other applications, such as to enable observation of [[Macroscopic quantum phenomena|quantum phenomena in macroscopic objects]].  Prominent results from her group in this area included the cooling of a [[centimeter]]-scale object to a temperature of 0.8 [[kelvin]] and the observation of a 2.7-[[kilogram]] [[pendulum]] near its quantum [[ground state]].  These experiments lay the foundations for observing quantum behavior in human-scale objects.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Berardelli|first1=Phil|title=Reflections of Absolute Zero|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/reflections-absolute-zero|work=Science|date=9 April 2007|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Press release: Laser-cooling brings large object near absolute zero|url=https://news.mit.edu/2007/super-cool|work=MIT News|date=5 April 2007}}</ref>

=== Quantum states of light ===

Mavalvala has also worked on the development of exotic quantum states of [[light]], and in particular the generation of light in squeezed coherent states.<ref name="LIGOnews11">Dave Reitze, [http://ligonews.blogspot.com/2011/10/squeezed-light-experiment-glowing.html Squeezed Light Experiment a Glowing Success!], ''LIGO Laboratory News'' (28 October 2011).</ref><ref name="Nature13">{{cite journal |last1=Andersen |first1=Ulrik L. |title=Squeezing more out of LIGO |journal=Nature Photonics |date=August 2013 |volume=7 |issue=8 |pages=589–590 |doi=10.1038/nphoton.2013.182|bibcode=2013NaPho...7..589A |s2cid=121670037 }}</ref> By injecting such states into the kilometre-scale [[Michelson interferometer]] of the LIGO detectors, her group greatly improved the sensitivity of the detector by reducing quantum noise;<ref name="Nature13" /> such squeezed states also have many other applications in experimental physics.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Walls |first1=D. F. |chapter=Generation and Applications of Squeezed Light |date=1994 |chapter-url=https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-79504-6_8 |title=Quantum Optics |pages=137–175 |editor-last=Walls |editor-first=D. F. |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-79504-6_8 |isbn=978-3-642-79504-6 |access-date=2022-10-08 |last2=Milburn |first2=G. J. |editor2-last=Milburn |editor2-first=G. J.|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> Her group was the first to generate squeezed light using optomechanics at room temperature,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Xuereb |first=André |date=July 2020 |title=Squeezing hots up |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-019-0770-7 |journal=Nature Physics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=710–711 |doi=10.1038/s41567-019-0770-7 |bibcode=2020NatPh..16..710X |s2cid=220507828 |issn=1745-2481|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Aggarwal |first1=Nancy |last2=Cullen |first2=Torrey J. |last3=Cripe |first3=Jonathan |last4=Cole |first4=Garrett D. |last5=Lanza |first5=Robert |last6=Libson |first6=Adam |last7=Follman |first7=David |last8=Heu |first8=Paula |last9=Corbitt |first9=Thomas |last10=Mavalvala |first10=Nergis |date=July 2020 |title=Room-temperature optomechanical squeezing |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41567-020-0877-x |journal=Nature Physics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=7 |pages=784–788 |doi=10.1038/s41567-020-0877-x |arxiv=2006.14323 |bibcode=2020NatPh..16..784A |s2cid=119453105 |issn=1745-2481}}</ref> compared to all previous optomechanical squeezed light sources that operated at [[Cryogenics|cryogenic]] (very low) temperatures.

==Personal life==

Mavalvala is a [[lesbian]] and speaks openly on her sexual orientation and family history as a Pakistani immigrant, describing herself as an "out, queer person of color."<ref name=":0">{{cite news |last1=Venkatraman |first1=Vijaysree |date=1 June 2012 |title=Gravitational wave researcher succeeds by being herself |language=en |work=Science |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/gravitational-wave-researcher-succeeds-being-herself |doi=10.1126/science.caredit.a1200061}}</ref> Mavalvala stated that she was not aware of her sexual orientation until after college. Mavalvala is frequently questioned about how she was able to break through the barrier of [[gender role]]s and pursue a career of her choice. In an interview with the Pakistani newspaper [[DAWN (newspaper)|''Dawn,'']] Mavalvala states, "I grew up in a family where the stereotypical gender roles were not really observed. So I grew up thinking women can, must and should do anything and everything. That is very important for me."<ref name=":2" /> She also speaks about the ability of individuals in Pakistan to break gender roles and stigmas: "Anybody should be able to do those things. And I am proof of that because I am all of those things. With the right combination of opportunity, it was possible for me to do."<ref name=":0" />

Mavalvala is often viewed as a role model for aspiring female scientists with roots in the [[Indian subcontinent|South Asia]]. As a young child Mavalvala was frequently involved in handy work, and was not bound to stereotypical gender roles in subcontinent culture, due to the manner in which her sister and she were raised. Mavalvala states that much of her success is accredited to good mentors in both the United States and Pakistan that encouraged her academic ability. In a television interview in 2016, Mavalvala stated, "When everyone has access to education that's when all the other things come into place... [You've] got to do what gives you pleasure, gotta find a way to do it. People should just do what they enjoy most and I think for all of society whether it's in Pakistan or elsewhere we have to create opportunities for young girls to do what they're good at and do what they love to do must cultivate the sense of wonder in a child."<ref>Neo Tv Network - Exclusive Interview Of Nerjis Mavalvala [Television broadcast]. (17 February 2016). In News. Karachi, Pakistan: Neo TV.</ref>

Mavalvala and her partner have two children and reside in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] in the United States. Mavalvala has extended family in Karachi and visited the city in 2010.<ref name="ScienceMag" /><ref name="DAWN" /><ref name="Express Tribune">{{cite web |date=15 February 2016 |title=Karachi bike repairman inspired Mavalvala |url=http://tribune.com.pk/story/1047678/karachi-bike-repairman-inspired-mavalvala/ |access-date=18 February 2016 |website=Express Tribune}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Meet The Queer Woman Who Proved Einstein's Theory About Gravitational Waves |url=http://www.newnownext.com/meet-the-queer-woman-who-proved-einsteins-theory-about-gravitational-waves/02/2016/ |access-date=19 February 2016 |website=NewNowNext}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Interview of Nargis Mavalvala |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1vfceLjs3lU |access-date=6 April 2016 |website=YouTube| date=16 February 2016 }}</ref>

She visited Cedar College (a prominent A Level School) on the 23rd of September 2026, in Karachi, Pakistan; giving a lecture on "The Quest for Gravitational Waves".
